extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of combustion turbine EGUs, power sector developers, state and federal regulators, and EPA rule commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the EPA's final standards, subcategorization thresholds, BSER determinations, and related implementation rules for new and reconstructed stationary combustion turbines under the NSPS (40 CFR part 60, subparts TTTT and TTTTa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategory electric sales thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The 12-operating-month electric sales (capacity factor) thresholds that define combustion turbine subcategories in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 — Low Load: ≤20 percent; Intermediate Load: >20 and ≤40 percent; Base Load: >40 percent of potential electric sales. These thresholds determine which BSER and corresponding standard of performance apply to a combustion turbine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low load subcategory definition and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Low load subcategory includes combustion turbines that operate only during periods of peak electric demand (i.e., peaking units) and provide ramping and ancillary services; they generally operate for short periods and at relatively low duty cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this operation increases variability in emissions rates and reduces ability to set meaningful output-based standards, the EPA found it difficult to establish a reasonable output-based standard for low load turbines. The Agency finalized a low load electric sales threshold of 20 percent to distinguish low load from intermediate load turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for low load subcategory
rubrics_metrics.description: For the low load (peaking) subcategory, the EPA determined the best system of emission reduction (BSER) is the use of lower-emitting fuels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPA proposed and is finalizing that the use of fuels with an emissions rate of less than 160 lb CO2/MMBtu meets the BSER requirements for the low load subcategory. This reflects technical feasibility (natural gas is the predominant low-emitting fuel) and the difficulty of applying an output-based standard to frequently ramping/peaking units. (Note: the 2015 NSPS used a heat-input based standard of 120 lb CO2/MMBtu for non-base load units; the current final decision references fuels <160 lb CO2/MMBtu.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate load subcategory definition and thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate load combustion turbines are those selling greater than 20 percent and less than or equal to 40 percent of their potential electric output (12-operating-month electric sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed sliding-scale approaches were considered (different thresholds for simple cycle vs combined cycle), but the final rule uses the fixed >20–≤40% threshold for intermediate load classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for intermediate load subcategory
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is finalizing as the BSER for the intermediate load subcategory: highly efficient generating technology—simple cycle technology—and operating and maintaining it efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agency considered multi-component BSERs (including co-firing low-GHG hydrogen phased in by certain dates) but is not finalizing a second component or phase-2 standard of performance for intermediate load turbines at this time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base load subcategory definition and threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Base load combustion turbines are those selling greater than 40 percent of their potential electric output (12-operating-month electric sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turbines above the 40% threshold are placed in the base load subcategory and are subject to the base load BSER and phased standards of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for base load subcategory and phased compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is finalizing a two-component BSER for base load turbines: (1) phase-1: highly efficient combined cycle generation and efficient operation/maintenance; (2) phase-2: highly efficient combined cycle generation plus 90 percent CCS beginning in 2032.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal had multiple pathways including hydrogen co-firing and different phase-in dates; the final rule does not finalize hydrogen co-firing as a BSER component for base load turbines. Owners/operators of new/reconstructed base load turbines must meet phase-1 on initial startup and meet the phase-2 standard of performance for 12-operating-month rolling averages beginning on or after January 2032, reflecting application of both components (including 90% CCS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale and data-based choice of electric sales thresholds (20% low load)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated capacity-factor/electric-sales thresholds (10%, 15%, 20%, 25%) and determined 10% was problematic due to high variability in emission rates; emission rates begin to stabilize above 15 percent and clearly stabilize above 20 percent for most simple cycle turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finalized a fixed 20 percent low load threshold because it represents a utilization level where most simple cycle turbines show consistent efficiency and GHG performance, enabling an output-based standard reflecting BSER while being more environmentally protective than higher thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated onsite renewable generation treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The rated output of integrated renewables is included when determining the design efficiency of the affected facility and is included in determining the NSPS emissions rate, but the output from integrated renewables is not included when determining net electric sales for subcategorization applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA decided not to count integrated renewables toward electric sales for subcategorization because including them could discourage integrated renewables (or curtailments) by shifting units into subcategories with more stringent emissions standards. Including integrated renewables in design efficiency slightly increases allowable electric sales for subcategorization purposes and lowers the facility emissions rate by about 1 percent. Commenters generally supported including renewables in determining emissions rate and design efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated energy storage treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will include the rated output of energy storage when determining the design efficiency of the affected facility, but the output from energy storage is not considered in determining the NSPS emissions rate nor counted as net electric sales for subcategorization applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: storage dispatches prior to the combustion turbine, likely lowering turbine capacity factors, but charging source is uncertain (could be high- or low-emitting). Therefore, storage output is not counted toward emissions rate or subcategorization net sales. EPA may evaluate storage impacts further in future rulemaking (e.g., if starts/stops reduced and efficiency increased, thresholds might be reconsidered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and documentation of system emergency and exclusion from subcategorization
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is including a clarified 'system emergency' concept: hours of operation during declared system emergencies (EEA levels 2 and 3) are excluded from the percentage electric sales subcategorization threshold; EEA level 1 is excluded from the definition of 'system emergency'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA agrees the definition should not be limited to EGUs not operating when the emergency is declared (i.e., it applies to EGUs already operating). Commenters asked to align terminology with NERC (balancing authority or reliability coordinator). The intent is that the local grid operator determines EGUs essential to reliability. Operators should determine and document generation during system emergencies. Excluding EEA levels 2 and 3 helps ensure operational flexibility during energy-deficient, time-limited events; level 1 events are more frequent/longer and often don't reflect an actual energy deficiency, so including level 1 would risk increased GHGs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate standard of performance during system emergencies (CCS exemption)
rubrics_metrics.description: During system emergencies, owners/operators of EGUs equipped with CCS may temporarily reduce capture or cease capture and instead be subject to a BSER based on the combustion of lower-emitting fuels; emissions and output during the emergency hours are not included when calculating the 12-operating-month emissions rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA determined an alternate efficiency-based emissions standard was not feasible because system emergencies are short/infrequent and not representative of longer-term achievable emissions rates; CCS systems have high start/stop costs and energy requirements, so allowing temporary reduction/cessation of capture during emergencies maintains reliability without treating operators as violating environmental requirements. Note DOE section 202(c) orders also deem operation pursuant to such orders not in violation of environmental requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-fuel-fired turbines: subcategory treatment and adjusted standards
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not including a separate multi-fuel subcategory for low, intermediate, and base load combustion turbines; new multi-fuel-fired turbines commencing construction/reconstruction after May 23, 2023, will be placed into the low/intermediate/base subcategory based on their level of electric sales, and the performance standards for each subcategory will be adjusted to reflect application of the BSER to turbines burning fuels with higher GHG emission rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background: in 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT, multi-fuel-fired units were those combusting ≥10% non-natural gas fuels on a 12-operating-month rolling average. To avoid circumvention (e.g., burning 10% fuel oil to remain subject to a less stringent multi-fuel standard), EPA removes the multi-fuel subcategory for new units and instead adjusts subcategory performance standards (heat-input-based standards) to reflect higher-emitting fuels. To be consistent with 2015 NSPS lower-emitting fuels definition, the maximum allowable heat-input based emissions rate is 160 lb CO2/MMBtu; EPA gives example that an efficient-generation standard would be ~33% higher for fuel-oil-fired turbines versus natural-gas-fired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of multi-fuel circumvention
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA identified potential circumvention where owners/operators of simple cycle turbines could elect to burn ≥10% non-natural gas fuels (e.g., Nos. 1 or 2 fuel oil) to remain in the multi-fuel subcategory and thereby be subject to a less stringent standard, enabling less efficient designs to operate as base load without efficiency improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid higher emissions and circumvention, EPA is finalizing that the multi-fuel subcategory will not apply for new units and standards will be adjusted by subcategory and fuel GHG intensity so efficient generation BSER applies across fuels while accounting for fuel carbon content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and alignment with reliability constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA expects system emergency determination and documentation to align with reliability constructs (e.g., NERC terminology such as balancing authority or reliability coordinator) and to be determined by local grid operators (RTO/ISO or balancing authority/reliability coordinator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters recommended deleting 'abnormal' and aligning terms with NERC; EPA accepted clarifications and applied definition to both subpart TTTT and final subpart TTTTa to ensure consistent implementation. The Agency's definition includes EEA levels 2 and 3 and applies to all EGUs, whether already operating or not.
